chapter.title: The toll on the way out, and the traps

cards.body: Keep a share 13 months instead of 11, and your tax bill can drop to zero. Every bazaar has an exit gate, and this one has a toll booth: **the longer you stayed inside, the smaller the toll**. Just outside the gate, touts shout about faster ways to get rich.
cards.simpler: Selling a share is like walking out of a bazaar through a gate with a toll booth. The toll is the tax on your profit. **The longer you stayed inside, the smaller the toll.** Keep a share 13 months instead of 11, and your tax bill can drop to zero. Just outside the gate, people shout about faster ways to get rich.

cards.prompt: Asha and Kabir buy the same share on the same day. Each one sells for a ₹10,000 profit. Asha sells in month 11 and Kabir in month 13. Who pays the smaller toll at the gate?

options.text: Asha: she left sooner, so there was less to tax
Kabir: he stayed past a year

whyNot.a: That mixes up leaving early with staying long. The toll gets smaller the longer you stay, not the sooner you go.
whyNot.c: That only looks at the profit and ignores the calendar. Two identical gains can carry very different tolls.

cards.reteach: The exit toll is set mostly by the calendar. Stay in the bazaar for more than 12 months and the gate charges less. Leave earlier and it charges more, even on exactly the same profit.

cards.title: The calendar sets the toll
cards.body:
When you sell a share for more than you paid, the profit is called a *capital gain*, and the government takes a cut at the gate. **How big the cut is depends on how long you held the share.**

Keep it 12 months or less and the gain is *short-term*: taxed at 20%. Keep it longer than 12 months and it's *long-term*: taxed at 12.5%, and only on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year (April to March). *A 4% cess, a small extra charge, is added to the tax. We'll leave it out of the maths here.*

You'd think the toll depends on how much you made. First, it depends on how long you waited.
cards.simpler: When you sell a share for more than you paid, the profit is a capital gain, and the government taxes it. **How much tax you pay depends on how long you held the share.** Held 12 months or less, it counts as short-term and is taxed at 20%. Held longer, it counts as long-term and is taxed at 12.5%, but only on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a year running April to March. There's also a small extra 4% charge, which we skip here.

cards.title: Priya's two months
cards.body: Priya in Pune buys 10 shares of a Nifty 50 bank at ₹1,500 each, so ₹15,000 in total. Eleven months later they're worth ₹2,000 each: a ₹5,000 gain. If she sells now, the short-term toll is 20% of ₹5,000, which is ₹1,000. If she waits two more months and the price stays put, the gain becomes long-term and sits well under the ₹1.25 lakh tax-free amount. Tax: ₹0. Same shares and same profit, a thousand rupees apart, **all decided by the calendar**.
cards.simpler: Priya in Pune buys 10 shares of a big Nifty 50 bank at ₹1,500 each, so ₹15,000 in all. Eleven months later each share is worth ₹2,000, a ₹5,000 profit. If she sells now, the short-term tax is 20%, or ₹1,000. If she waits two more months and the price stays the same, the profit becomes long-term and is well under the ₹1.25 lakh tax-free amount. Tax: ₹0. Same shares, same profit, ₹1,000 apart, **all decided by the calendar**.

cards.prompt: Meera has a ₹1,45,000 gain on shares she bought 10 months ago. She won't need the money this year, and she has no other gains. Which plan works out the toll correctly?

options.text: Sell now: she owes 20% on only ₹20,000, because the first ₹1.25 lakh is free
Wait 3 months: then she owes 12.5% of ₹20,000, which is ₹2,500, instead of ₹29,000 now
Wait 3 months: then the whole ₹1,45,000 is tax-free because it's long-term

whyNot.a: That uses the long-term tax-free amount on a short-term sale. Sold at 10 months, the whole ₹1,45,000 is taxed at 20%, which is ₹29,000.
whyNot.c: That stretches the tax-free amount too far. Only the first ₹1.25 lakh of long-term gains each year is free. The other ₹20,000 is taxed at 12.5%.

cards.reteach: It takes two steps. First, check the calendar: 12 months or less means 20% on the whole gain. More than 12 months means you take ₹1.25 lakh off the year's long-term gains, then pay 12.5% on whatever is left.

cards.title: The touts at the gate
cards.body:
Outside the gate, someone is always selling a shortcut. A Telegram group promises a 'target price' by Friday. A friend's cousin swears that options are where the real money is.

There's a plain reason tips fail. Burton Malkiel is known for arguing that short-term price moves are close to unpredictable, so the person sending the tip can't see Friday either. *Futures and options* (F&O) are bets on where a price will be by a fixed date. SEBI's own 2023 study found that **nearly 9 in 10 individual F&O traders lost money**.

Three things to say no to in your first year: tips, F&O, and selling within 12 months without a real reason.
cards.simpler: Outside the gate, people sell shortcuts: a Telegram group's 'target price' by Friday, or a cousin's tip about options. Burton Malkiel is known for arguing that short-term price moves are close to unpredictable, so tipsters can't see Friday either. Futures and options (F&O) are bets on a price by a set date, and the market regulator SEBI found in 2023 that **nearly 9 in 10 individual F&O traders lost money**. Year one: no tips, no F&O, no selling within 12 months without good reason.

cards.body: Rohan bought shares at ₹800. Eleven months later he was nicely up when a WhatsApp group posted: book your profit and move into the next big winner before Monday. He sold, paid the 20% short-term toll, and the new pick fell that same week. How to spot it: **when a message gives you a deadline shorter than your own plan, that's the tout talking**, and the toll booth is listening.
cards.simpler: Rohan bought shares at ₹800. Eleven months later he was well up when a WhatsApp group posted: take your profit and jump into the next big winner before Monday. He sold, paid the 20% short-term tax, and the new pick fell that same week. The warning sign: **when a message gives you a deadline shorter than your own plan, that's the pushy seller talking**, and the toll booth is listening.

cards.prompt: A friend asks how tax works when you sell shares at a profit. Which one-line answer gets it right?

options.text: Sell before a year is up, because the short-term rate is the lower one
It depends on how long you held: a year or less is 20%, longer is 12.5%, after the first ₹1.25 lakh of long-term gains each year
It's a flat 20% on every gain, so waiting changes nothing

whyNot.a: That's the hurry the touts sell, not the rule. Short-term gains carry the higher rate, 20%.
whyNot.c: That's only the short-term rate. After 12 months the rate drops to 12.5%, and the tax-free amount kicks in.

cards.reteach: Picture a toll booth with two lanes. The fast lane is for anyone who held 12 months or less, and it charges 20%. The slow lane is for anyone who held longer: it lets the first ₹1.25 lakh of gains each year through free and charges 12.5% on the rest.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
When you sell a share at a profit, the calendar sets the toll: held 12 months or less, you pay 20% of the gain; held longer, you pay 12.5%, and only on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year. **The traps at the gate, tips and F&O, all push you to hurry, and hurrying is exactly what costs you.**

Next: two banks, five numbers, and which shop you'd rather own.
cards.simpler: When you sell a share at a profit, the calendar sets the toll. Held 12 months or less, you pay 20% of the gain. Held longer, you pay 12.5%, and only on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year. **The traps at the gate, tips and F&O, all push you to hurry, and hurrying is exactly what costs you.** Next: two banks, five numbers, and which shop you'd rather own.

cards.body: Open the holdings page in your broker app and pick one share. Note the date you bought it, then write down the first date you'll have held it for more than 12 months. That's the day its toll drops.
cards.simpler: Open the app you use to buy shares and go to the page that lists the shares you own. Pick one. Note the date you bought it, then write down the first day you'll have held it for more than 12 months. **That's the day its toll drops.** Like marking a birthday on a calendar, you'll know exactly when waiting pays off.
